claims.text: The intervention changes Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 to Fe22Ni16Co19Mn12Cr16P15, reducing P and Mn while increasing Fe and Co.
The modified Fe22Ni16Co19Mn12Cr16P15 alloy was prepared from at least 99.9 wt.% elemental powders by arc melting and repeated remelting.
The modified alloy is available as both a slower-cooled arc-melted ingot and an approximately 20 μm melt-spun ribbon.
Reducing phosphorus to 15 at.% while adjusting the Fe/Co/Mn ratios will improve glass-forming ability relative to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
The same composition change will increase the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The composition change promotes a eutectic-dominated solidification pathway.
The eutectic-dominated pathway suppresses primary crystallization and high-temperature phosphide formation.
The relevant eutectic-dominated microstructure contains fine, predominantly rod-like eutectic colonies.
Under rapid quenching, the modified composition yields a fully amorphous ribbon rather than a multiphase crystalline structure.
Reduced phosphorus and adjusted transition-metal ratios decrease the tendency for primary solid-solution crystallization.
Cooperative eutectic growth suppresses elemental segregation and crystal-nucleation events.
Rapid cooling amplifies the proposed suppression of segregation and nucleation, promoting amorphization.
The modified melt-spun alloy should have a delayed crystallization onset and a wider thermal-stability interval on reheating than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy should exhibit a simpler, eutectic-type devitrification sequence than the baseline alloy.
The baseline Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy previously exhibited multiple crystallization events attributed to eutectic, primary, and non-eutectic nucleation under slower cooling.
The proposed improvements are expected in approximately 20 μm ribbons produced by rapid melt spinning at about 40 m/s.
Slower-cooled arc-melted bulk samples are likely to crystallize into multiple phases because they allow sufficient time for elemental partitioning.
The observed thermal-stability improvement may depend on cooling rate and heating protocol.
